LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Donkey — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands your toddler the deck’s comedy crown: hee-haw, sung slowly, sung fast, sung gloomy — a one-sound song that teaches how words are built from bits.

What is this?

A donkey is a long-eared farm animal that says hee-haw — a two-part bray that starts high and ends low, which is why it sounds so gloriously wrong.

What does it mean?

Hee-haw is high-low in one breath: your toddler is singing an interval without knowing it. Two-part sounds teach that noises have shape, the seed of all later speech melody.

What does the child need to know?

Deliver it slow and gloomy at least once — the droopy version is reliably the one that lands the laugh. Nobody is more delighted by the silliness than the toddler.

Why this matters

One sound, many performances: hee-haw teaches a toddler that a noise can be stretched, shuffled and staged — the discovery that words are built from parts.

What it teaches

Pitch play from high to low, song-building with a single syllable pair, and comic timing — the first jokes toddlers tell are sound jokes they control.

Words to learn

donkeyhee-hawfunnylongearssong

Say this to your child

“"A donkey! Hee-haw! Can you say it? Hee — haw! Now slowly… heeeee… haaaaaw. The donkey owns the silliest noise on the whole farm, and very, very long ears."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say donkey, then hee-haw — high on hee, low on haw, with the long ears drooping.
  2. Sing it three ways together: fast hee-haw, slow hee-haw, and the gloomy one that ends in a sigh.
  3. Invent a hee-haw song where every verse finishes with the bray — any farm tune you half-remember will carry it.
  4. When your toddler invents a new way to say it — extra haws, double hees — adopt their version immediately; their composition is the milestone.
  5. Assign hee-haw its jobs this week: it opens the toy box, it greets the bath, it finishes the bedtime book.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows a donkey saying hee-haw. Find the donkey, find the hee-haw, then ask where the donkey’s ears are — long ears are this card’s best detail.

Ask your child

"Where is the donkey?" "What does the donkey say?" "Can you say it slow and gloomy?" "Can you make up a hee-haw song?"

What your child can say or do

"Hee-HAW!" with a droopy face, or a haw that arrives without the hee — take it. Some toddlers will hee-haw every animal for a day; the donkey’s fame is brief and glorious.

Out in the real world

Donkeys appear at farms, on the beach in some towns, and in every nursery-song book. The beach or paddock version gets the loudest toddler hee-haw on record.

Try it together

Hee-haw choir: every family member picks a different hee-haw speed and you sing them in order — fast, slow, gloomy, sleepy. Your toddler conducts and chooses which comes next.

Understanding check

Ask what the donkey says. Any hee, haw or haw-hee passes. The real test is the invented variation — a hee-hee-haw or a sung-gloomy haw means sound play has gone creative.

Parent tips

Match their tempo once, then offer one alternative — fast after slow, quiet after loud. The contrast is what keeps a one-sound game alive past the third day.

Staying safe

Farm donkeys look soft and are stronger than they act — feed nothing, stroke nothing without the farmer’s yes, and keep fingers away from those long, curious lips.

This lesson pairs with the Donkey flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).
